:::{#exm-edf-gaussian}
#### The Gaussian distribution in exponential dispersion form

For a Gaussian outcome $Y \sim \ndist{\mu, \sigma^2}$:

$$
\ba
f(y; \mu, \sigma^2)
&= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \expf{-\frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}
&& \text{(Gaussian density)}
\\ &= \expf{-\frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{1}{2}\logf{2\pi\sigma^2}}
&& \text{(write the constant as the exponential of its log)}
\\ &= \expf{-\frac{y^2 - 2y\mu + \mu^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{1}{2}\logf{2\pi\sigma^2}}
&& \text{(expand the square)}
\\ &= \expf{\frac{y\mu - \mu^2/2}{\sigma^2} - \frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{1}{2}\logf{2\pi\sigma^2}}
&& \text{(split the fraction)}
\ea
$$

Matching this last line to @def-exponential-dispersion-family gives
$\theta \eqdef \mu$,
$b(\theta) \eqdef \theta^2/2$,
$\phi \eqdef \sigma^2$,
and
$c(y, \phi) \eqdef -\frac{y^2}{2\phi} - \frac{1}{2}\logf{2\pi\phi}$.

For instance, take $\mu = 2$, $\sigma^2 = 4$, and $y = 3$.
The first term of the exponent is

$$
\ba
\frac{y\theta - b(\theta)}{\phi}
&= \frac{3 \cdot 2 - 2^2/2}{4}
&& \text{(substitute } y = 3,\ \theta = 2,\ \phi = 4\text{)}
\\ &= \frac{6 - 2}{4}
&& \text{(multiply and square)}
\\ &= 1
&& \text{(subtract and divide)}
\ea
$$

and the second term is
$c(3, 4) = -\frac{9}{8} - \frac{1}{2}\logf{8\pi}$,
so the exponent is $-\frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{2}\logf{8\pi}$.
The Gaussian density's own exponent is also
$-\frac{(3 - 2)^2}{8} - \frac{1}{2}\logf{8\pi} = -\frac{1}{8} - \frac{1}{2}\logf{8\pi}$,
and both forms give $f(3) \approx 0.1760$.
:::
